content: Palliative care is not only about alleviating suffering but also about ensuring continuity of care for individuals with chronic conditions and maintaining the comfort and dignity of patients who are not expected to survive. In any humanitarian emergency or crisis, responses should adhere to the Humanitarian Charter of the Sphere Project and the humanitarian principles of the Red Cross. Ethical principles from organizations like the ICRC and MSF also provide valuable guidance. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines palliative care as the prevention and relief of suffering for adult and pediatric patients, as well as their families, who are dealing with life-threatening illnesses. This suffering can be physical, psychological, social, or spiritual, and it extends to the family members of the patient. Palliative care involves early identification, thorough assessment, and treatment of these issues. It aims to enhance quality of life, promote dignity and comfort, and may even positively influence the course of the illness. It is applicable early in the disease process, alongside life-prolonging therapies, and provides support to both patients and families throughout the illness. After the patient’s death, it continues to support bereaved family members. Palliative care is not merely an alternative to disease-modifying treatments at the end of life. Instead, it should be integrated with prevention, early diagnosis, and treatment of serious or life-limiting health problems at all levels of the healthcare system. This integration improves continuity of care and strengthens health systems. Additionally, palliative care seeks to mitigate the harmful effects of poverty on patients and families, protecting them from financial hardship due to illness or disability. It encourages active involvement from communities and their members. Importantly, integrating palliative care into public health systems is essential for achieving universal health coverage. The specific types, scale, and severity of suffering vary depending on geopolitical location, economic situation, culture, and the nature of the emergency or crisis. People in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) are more vulnerable to unnecessary suffering due to limited access to disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and social support compared to those in high-income countries (HICs). Consequently, the need for palliative care is greater in LMICs, and the required services may differ. Suffering associated with chronic life-threatening illnesses can also occur acutely or in connection with non-life-threatening conditions. In settings where relief of acute or non-life-threatening suffering is inadequate or unavailable, clinicians trained in palliative care should intervene by training colleagues in symptom control, providing direct symptom relief, or both. For example, in countries where pain medicine is not yet a specialty, the prevention and relief of pain from trauma, burns, or surgery are often inadequate, especially during and after disasters and conflicts when healthcare services may be scarce or unavailable. Clinicians trained in palliative care can help address this therapeutic gap. Many countries also lack rehabilitation medicine specialists and programs to care for individuals with serious disabilities, such as paraplegia, quadriplegia, brain injuries, or congenital anomalies. Palliative care can help fill this void as well. Planning and implementing palliative care services should be based on an assessment of the types and extent of inadequately prevented or relieved physical, psychological, social, or spiritual suffering in adults and children. Only through such assessments can palliative care services be tailored to local needs and the needs of individual patients and families, ensuring a people-centered approach. People affected by different types of emergencies or crises, such as earthquakes, major storms, hemorrhagic fever epidemics, or political violence, may suffer in different ways and require different types of care. However, several principles apply to palliative care in any humanitarian emergency or crisis. The most fundamental goal of palliative care, and medicine in general, is to relieve human suffering. While saving lives is a crucial way to achieve this goal, it is not the only way. Humanitarian responses to emergencies and crises must include palliative care and symptom control. Responses that exclude palliative care are medically deficient and ethically indefensible. In humanitarian emergencies and crises, clinicians, including those trained in palliative care, should make every effort to save the lives of patients who may be savable. The only exception should be patients with pre-existing chronic life-threatening conditions who have decided and left clear instructions to forego life-sustaining treatment. Palliative care never intentionally hastens death but provides necessary treatments to achieve an adequate level of comfort for the patient, respecting their values. In rare cases of severe, refractory symptoms in terminally ill patients, ensuring comfort may unintentionally but foreseeably hasten death, in line with the ethical principle of double effect. Palliative care and life-saving treatment should not be regarded as distinct. Instead, palliative care and symptom control should be integrated as much as possible with life-saving treatment for patients with acute life-threatening conditions. Palliative care should commence immediately for patients with non-life-threatening conditions whose treatment may be delayed. It must also be provided for all patients deemed expectant and should begin without delay. Standard triage categorization in humanitarian emergencies often overlooks palliative care and symptom relief, suggesting that expectant patients require even less attention than those with minor health conditions. A more medically and ethically sound categorization integrates palliative care into all levels of triage, ensuring that symptom relief and comfort are provided to all patients, regardless of their prognosis. In humanitarian emergencies, the prevention and relief of suffering should be accessible to anyone experiencing physical, psychological, social, or spiritual distress, not just those with life-threatening conditions. However, there is a particular ethical imperative to provide palliative care and symptom control for expectant patients. This imperative is based on the principles of beneficence and non-abandonment. Failure to address the suffering of these highly vulnerable patients constitutes abandonment and is ethically unacceptable. Pain is the most common and severe type of suffering in many humanitarian emergencies and crises. Treating pain aggressively is crucial for all patients, including those with trauma and postoperative conditions. Inadequate pain control can lead to a range of undesirable physiological and immunological effects, poor surgical outcomes, and increased risk of chronic pain and psychological distress. Therefore, failure to treat pain aggressively in patients triaged as red or yellow constitutes substandard care and is both medically and ethically unacceptable. To provide palliative care and symptom control in humanitarian emergencies, a package of safe, effective, and inexpensive palliative medicines and equipment is required, along with at least basic training for response team members. Most healthcare providers in humanitarian response teams and local clinicians can be trained to provide adequate palliative care for most patients and families. However, in some situations, the presence of a palliative care specialist with training in disaster medicine may be beneficial to manage complex symptoms and help integrate sustainable palliative care services into the local healthcare system. In natural disasters such as earthquakes, many patients may die weeks after the event due to complications like infections or organ failure. Palliative care should be an integral part of humanitarian responses to address the suffering of these patients. Similarly, tsunamis can devastate social and medical infrastructure, causing widespread suffering and health problems. Palliative care is essential in these contexts to provide symptom control and psychosocial support for patients with non-survivable injuries or illnesses.
